title: Creative Thinking
description: Editable version of the complete Mayne Leadership Creative Thinking course, including its original explanations, practice activities, application, and reflection prompts.
author: Joshua Mayne

Creative thinking is not about being artistic. It is about deliberately finding possibilities that routine thinking misses.
Challenge assumptions. Change the question. Generate more than the obvious answer. Combine ideas. Develop what has promise. Test before you bet everything.
Approx. 2 hours · Full interactive course · Extended practice labs included · Progress saved on this device

This online course follows the full learning sequence: concrete experience, constrained thinking, curiosity, reframing, divergence, connection-making, structured creativity tools, elaboration, convergence, experimentation, and a culminating application.
Learning objectives
Explain the role of creative thinking in organizational problem solving.
Recognize assumptions and habits that constrain creativity.
Reframe problems to reveal alternative perspectives.
Generate multiple and diverse solutions using divergent-thinking techniques.
Apply structured creativity tools to organizational challenges.
Develop, evaluate, and test creative ideas for practical application.

blocks.title: Creative thinking has a specific job.

blocks.body: Good problem solving uses several modes of thought. Creativity expands possibilities; critical thinking evaluates them; decision-making commits to action.
What could we do?
Generate alternatives, challenge constraints, combine ideas, and find possibilities beyond the first answer.
What should we do?
Examine evidence, assumptions, logic, tradeoffs, and the quality of the options in front of you.
What will we do?
Move from understanding the problem to choosing, implementing, and learning from a course of action.
Creativity is not permission to ignore reality. It is permission to search more widely before reality is used to narrow the field.
CREATIVITY VS. INNOVATION
Creativity generates and develops useful possibilities. Innovation turns a promising idea into something implemented, adopted, or producing value.
“I'M NOT CREATIVE”
Creative thinking is not a personality label or artistic talent. Questioning, reframing, divergence, connection-making, elaboration, convergence, and testing are learnable behaviors.

blocks.title: Efficiency can quietly become a boundary.

blocks.body: Experience helps us recognize patterns quickly—but the same efficiency can make our thinking predictable. The goal is not to reject experience. It is to notice when familiar thinking has become the only thinking.
Mental models
Internal pictures of how the world works can become invisible rules.
Assumptions
Things treated as true even though they may not have been tested.
Functional fixedness
Seeing a tool, process, or role only in its familiar use.
Habit + expertise
Past success can narrow the search to approaches we already know.
Organizational norms
“That is how we do it here” can become a substitute for examination.
Fear of failure
People self-censor before an idea is developed enough to judge fairly.
Premature judgment
Evaluation begins before the group has generated meaningful variety.
Group conformity
Agreement can feel safer than exploring a different frame.

Reframing is not wordsmithing. A useful reframe changes what counts as a possible solution—for example, shifting from attendance to motivation, from an event to continuous learning, or from organizational delivery to employee pull.

SCAMPER changes the search pattern by deliberately prompting different kinds of transformation. Produce at least one idea for every letter.

blocks.title: S · Substitute
blocks.body: What could we replace?

blocks.title: C · Combine
blocks.body: What could we put together?

blocks.title: A · Adapt
blocks.body: What could we borrow or modify from somewhere else?

blocks.title: M · Modify
blocks.body: What could we increase, decrease, simplify, magnify, or change?

blocks.title: P · Put to another use
blocks.body: What existing resource could serve a different purpose?

blocks.title: E · Eliminate
blocks.body: What step, approval, handoff, or requirement could disappear?

blocks.title: R · Reverse / Rearrange
blocks.body: What happens if we change the order or reverse who initiates the process?
Now identify the two SCAMPER ideas with the most potential. The point is not that every prompt produces a great idea; each prompt changes the search pattern.
Reverse thinking
Design the opposite or worst result, then reverse the conditions.
Six Thinking Hats
Deliberately shift the mode of attention used to examine an idea.
Attribute listing
Break a product, service, or process into attributes and alter them one at a time.
Morphological analysis
Combine different dimensions or features systematically.
Constraint removal
Temporarily remove a presumed limitation and examine what becomes possible.
Worst Possible Idea
Generate deliberately bad ideas to expose constructive design principles.
OPTIONAL / ALTERNATE PRACTICE LAB
Design the worst employee onboarding experience you can imagine. Then reverse the failures into useful design principles.

blocks.title: MAKE IT TERRIBLE
blocks.body: No instructions? Conflicting guidance? Information overload? Make it intentionally bad.

blocks.title: REVERSE IT
blocks.body: What constructive principles appear when you reverse the failures?
An idea becomes useful when you can explain how it would actually work.

blocks.title: Make one idea concrete enough to examine.

blocks.body: Choose one idea from your earlier list and develop it. A vague idea is hard to evaluate; an elaborated idea can be improved, combined, or tested.

blocks.body: Who participates or benefits?

blocks.title: WHAT HAPPENS FIRST?
blocks.body: Describe the first visible step.

blocks.title: WHAT HAPPENS NEXT?
blocks.body: How does the process continue?

blocks.title: RESOURCES REQUIRED
blocks.body: What people, tools, time, or support are needed?

blocks.title: BEHAVIOR CHANGE
blocks.body: What would people have to do differently?

blocks.title: BIGGEST BARRIER
blocks.body: What could prevent it from working?

blocks.title: ASSUMPTION TO TEST
blocks.body: What are you assuming about people or the process?
Development turns “interesting” into “understandable.” Once an idea is concrete, you can compare it with alternatives and identify what needs to be tested.
Narrow deliberately. Criteria should shape selection before preference takes over.

blocks.title: Choose how you will judge ideas before choosing the idea.

blocks.body: Select at least three criteria that matter for this challenge.

blocks.title: Choose five criteria before narrowing ideas
blocks.body:
Choose five criteria, explain their importance, and carry them into the tournament.

  • Mission impact
  • Effectiveness
  • Feasibility
  • Time
  • Cost
  • Risk
  • Stakeholder acceptance
  • Policy / legal fit
Visible criteria make convergence more defensible. Strong teams can also combine useful elements from ideas that do not survive as stand-alone options.
Decision matrix
Score options against explicit weighted criteria.
Impact–effort grid
Compare likely value with the effort required.
Dot voting
Surface preferences quickly—but explain why ideas survived.
Pros / cons
Make tradeoffs visible before commitment.
Must / should / could
Separate essential requirements from desirable features.
Combine ideas
Convergence can create a hybrid rather than crown an unchanged winner.

blocks.title: Narrow without shutting down too early.

blocks.body: Carry your 20 ideas into a deliberate convergence sequence. Criteria come before preference, and elimination does not mean useful features must disappear.

blocks.title: WHAT VALUABLE ELEMENT MIGHT BE LOST?

blocks.body: Healthy convergence narrows without shutting down thinking too soon. A final concept may combine the strongest elements of several ideas.

blocks.title: Which idea has the strongest potential against your criteria?
Tournament: Select 1
blocks.body: Choose the concept with the strongest potential against your criteria.
Selection is not the end of creative thinking. A promising idea is still a hypothesis. The next question is what you need to learn before scaling it.

blocks.title: WHY THIS CONCEPT?
blocks.body: Explain why it is strongest against the criteria.

blocks.title: WHAT SHOULD IT BORROW FROM OTHER IDEAS?
blocks.body: Preserve any useful feature that should survive elimination.
Reduce the cost of learning. Test the idea before defending it.

blocks.title: What is the smallest test that would teach you something useful?

blocks.body: Do not launch organization-wide. Build a low-risk pilot with clear learning criteria.

blocks.title: ASSUMPTION TO TEST
blocks.body: What must be true for this idea to work?

blocks.title: SMALLEST USEFUL PILOT
blocks.body: Who, where, and for how long?

blocks.title: EVIDENCE TO COLLECT
blocks.body: What will you measure or observe?

blocks.title: RISKS TO CONTROL
blocks.body: What risk must the pilot limit or monitor?

blocks.title: CONTINUE / ADJUST / STOP
blocks.body: What result would change your next move?
A failed experiment is not automatically a failed effort. If the test produces useful information, it reduces uncertainty and improves the next version.

blocks.title: A repeatable process—not a bag of tricks.

blocks.body: You do not need every tool every time. The value is recognizing what kind of thinking the situation needs next.

blocks.title: Apply the entire process to one organizational challenge.

blocks.body: An organization is experiencing declining employee participation in voluntary professional development. Announcements, reminders, and supervisor encouragement have produced little improvement. Leadership wants a fundamentally different approach. Walk through how your thinking changes—not just the final answer.

blocks.body: What do we know? What still needs to be known?

blocks.title: 2 · ASSUMPTIONS

blocks.body: What outside pattern, industry, or concept changes the idea?

blocks.title: 7 · DEVELOP

blocks.title: HOW DID YOUR THINKING CHANGE?
blocks.body: What became visible only after using the process?
The goal is not a single “correct” solution. The goal is to demonstrate deliberate creative thinking and show how the problem, options, and final concept changed through the process.
Creativity is a discipline.
Creative thinking can be practiced deliberately; it is not reserved for people who identify as “creative.”
Better questions create better options.
The first problem statement is not automatically the most useful one.
Generate before you evaluate.
Premature judgment reduces fluency, flexibility, and originality.
Connections expand the search.
Analogies, combinations, and outside perspectives reveal patterns your normal context hides.
Criteria before preference.
Convergence works best when the standards are visible before a favorite solution takes over.
Testing is learning.
Small experiments reduce uncertainty before large commitments are made.

The next time a team says, “We have already tried everything,” do not immediately search for another answer. First ask whether you are still asking the same question.

Method note: established methods referenced in this course include SCAMPER, Six Thinking Hats, morphological analysis, Worst Possible Idea, analogical/forced connections, and related divergent-thinking practices. Course-specific activities such as The Impossible Redesign, Assumption Breaker, Reframe It Five Ways, the 20-Idea Challenge, and Idea Tournament are adapted learning exercises built around established creativity research and practice.
